$comment: SOURCE OF TRUTH for every PixelOven surface colour. Nothing else defines one.
Reconciled from the two consumers that had independently maintained their own
copies (harmony/homepage/configs/custom.css, lattice/frontend/app/globals.css).
They had converged on the SAME semantic ladder and diverged only on values, so
this is that ladder with one set of values chosen on measurable grounds:
- lattice's surface ramp is monotonic and geometrically spaced; harmony's
inverted (border-muted L=0.01879 sat BELOW surface-hover L=0.01961) and
stepped unevenly. Both ended on the same accent-border luminance (0.0724),
so lattice is the same ladder, correctly interpolated.
- `dim`: harmony's #817a99 scored 4.47:1 on surface, failing WCAG AA body by
0.03. lattice's #9089ab scores 5.48:1 and passes.
TWO SCHEMES. Every colour token carries `dark` and `light`. The names are
identical across them, so a consumer switches scheme, not vocabulary.
The light ramp was DERIVED, not eyeballed: each step was solved for the same
contrast against its own ground that the corresponding dark step has against
its ground, at the dark ramp's own hue (227deg, which the dark scale holds to
within 3deg across all ten steps). The two schemes are therefore perceptually
equivalent rather than merely both present.
Consequently the ladder ASCENDS in luminance on dark and DESCENDS on light. The
real invariant is that it moves monotonically AWAY FROM THE PAGE GROUND, which
is what the tests assert per scheme. This mirrors how GitHub's light theme
works — white canvas, grey subtle surfaces, darker borders.
NOT ONLY COLOUR. The groups below `font` — radius, type, ease, duration,
shadow, z — are scheme-independent: one `value`, no `dark`/`light`. They were
promoted from lattice's globals.css, which had reasoned them out and was the
only place they existed. The same argument that made the palette a package
makes them one: a second consumer would otherwise hand-author its own copy,
which is how the colour drift started.

surface.$comment: The elevation ramp. Monotonic in both schemes, in opposite directions.

void.use: the page ground; nothing sits behind it

base.use: cards, panels, the default raised plane

raised.use: popovers, menus, anything above a surface

border.$comment: Continues the same ramp — borders are the far end of the elevation scale.

strong.use: emphasis, focus rings on neutral elements

text.$comment: Each entry declares the ground it sits on, and is asserted against THAT ground rather than a assumed one. onAccent is white in both schemes because a violet fill does not flip with the page.

dim.use: de-emphasised text; still AA on surface

onAccent.use: text on an accent fill — white in BOTH schemes, unlike text.bright
onAccent.sameAs: text.bright on dark; the overlap is intentional, not a duplicate

$comment: The brand violet survives BOTH schemes unchanged — 4.59:1 on the light
surface, and the anchor of the dark scheme. Worth keeping deliberately: the
primary brand colour is literally the same value everywhere it appears.

deep.use: active and pressed states — a FILL, never a foreground

soft.use: accent text against the ground; the muted brand tone

$comment: Semantic, not decorative. The dark values are luminous and fail badly on a
light ground — teal #00f0d8 is 1.25:1 there — so light gets darkened variants
at the same hue, each solved to 4.5:1 rather than picked by eye.
`success` is also the brand teal and is used as one on marks. That overload is
deliberate; accent.soft is the neutral substitute if it ever confuses.

statusSurface.$comment: Tinted grounds for status callouts. Carry body text in both schemes.

font.$comment: Scheme-independent — a typeface does not change with the ground.

mono.value: "IBM Plex Mono", ui-monospace, SFMono-Regular, Consolas, "Liberation Mono", monospace
mono.use: the brand voice — code, labels, data, eyebrows

$comment: PROMOTED FROM lattice/frontend/app/globals.css, not invented here. These
four steps are in production, internally consistent, and their reasoning
was written down at the time. Promoting them is the same move the colour
ramp was: take the copy that is demonstrably right and make it the source.
Squarer than the set they replaced there (7/10/14). Four of five reference
systems put a CONTROL at 4px or below; a 10px radius on a 22px row curves
through half the row height and reads as consumer-soft. 4px reads as
precise, which is what a knowledge substrate should read as.
sm/base/lg are 4/8/12 — the 4px grid, and 7px never can be. `xs` is 3px and
deliberately is NOT on the grid: on a 16px chip a 4px corner is already a
quarter of the height. (lattice's comment claims all four are multiples of
4; that is wrong about xs, so the claim is not carried over with the values.)

xs.use: chips, tags, badges — the smallest enclosed shapes

base.use: panels and cards; the default radius

lg.use: modals and sheets — the largest enclosing shapes

$comment: The type ramp, promoted from lattice. Seven steps, each carrying all four
metrics a step actually needs: size, line-height, weight, tracking.
BASE IS 13px, NOT 14px. Mono at 13px sets 38 characters in a 320px panel
where 14px sets 35, and this family of products is overwhelmingly
identifiers in narrow columns.
LINE HEIGHTS ARE INTEGER PX, never unitless ratios. A ratio produces
sub-pixel line boxes that break the 4px rhythm and make grouped lists
drift down the page. 13/18 is body copy here, not 14/1.6.
TRACKING RISES AS SIZE FALLS: -0.02em at display, +0.12em at micro. That is
what makes small mono read as deliberate rather than cramped, and it is
asserted rather than left to taste.
`weight` and `letterSpacing` are spelled out on EVERY step, including the
four places lattice left them to the browser default (400 and 0em). Same
rendered result; a component author should not have to know which steps
happen to omit one. The step carries the `use`; its four metrics are named
for what they are.
Sizes are px, not rem, to match the source they came from. A surface that
wants user-font-size scaling uses the additive reading group instead
of converting compact metrics locally — that is the drift this package prevents.

display.use: the one heading on a page; hero numerals

subtitle.use: a heading inside a panel; the lead line of a card

body.use: the default — running text, list rows, field values

ui.use: dense chrome: toolbars, breadcrumbs, table cells

micro.use: the smallest legible step: badges, counts, timestamps

reading.$comment: Additive scalable reading roles. rem metrics produce the approved px values at a 16px root and scale with user font preferences. The seven compact type roles remain byte-compatible. Use existing type.display/title with font.sans for headings; browser zoom scales those px headings.

body.use: explanations, search results and readable prose

input.use: search and readable text entry; preserve browser zoom

code.use: literal source and long canonical identifiers; wrap ordinary paths

fontFamily.value: "IBM Plex Mono", ui-monospace, SFMono-Regular, Consolas, "Liberation Mono", monospace

graphOrigin.$comment: Promoted from Lattice 8577b414: dark is unchanged. Light preserves the teal/amber/violet/rose families. Four typed hues retain >=15 CIEDE2000 separation, the neutral >=12, under normal/protanopic/deuteranopic/tritanopic vision. Opaque graphical marks only: use text tokens for labels. Rendering opacity and lighting need a separate consumer contrast replay.

wikilink.use: neutral stored wikilink edge; solid pattern

embed.use: embedded-note edge; teal family, solid pattern

tag.use: shared-tag connection; amber family, solid pattern

dataview.use: computed Dataview edge; violet family, solid pattern remains under reduced motion

frontmatterRef.use: frontmatter-reference edge; rose family, solid pattern

canvas.use: canvas edge; must use dashed DOM strokes or curved 3D links

wikilink.use: solid origin encoding; retain when motion is reduced

embed.use: solid origin encoding; retain when motion is reduced

tag.use: solid origin encoding; retain when motion is reduced

dataview.use: solid origin encoding; retain when motion is reduced

frontmatterRef.use: solid origin encoding; retain when motion is reduced

canvas.use: canvas secondary encoding; dashed in DOM, map to curvature in 3D

graph.$comment: Renderer roles. Ground and radiance are explicitly distinguished from foregrounds. Dimmed context is nonessential and cannot carry a label, selectable target or the only representation of a connection. Graph node degree describes the loaded projection, never corpus orphan status.

canvas.use: graph clear colour and fog ground

node.use: default opaque node; neutral so origins own the hue channel

nodeHub.use: high loaded-degree node; reinforce with size, never infer corpus degree

nodeIsolated.use: node with no links in the loaded projection; does not claim corpus orphan status

nodeSelected.use: selected opaque node; pair with visible identity and selection shape

nodeHover.use: hovered opaque node; pair with visible identity, never make hover the only access

nodeDimmed.use: nonessential out-of-focus node context only; no readable-contrast claim

edgeDimmed.use: nonessential out-of-focus edge context only; no readable-contrast claim

labelSurface.use: opaque selected and hover label ground

labelText.use: selected and hover identity text on the opaque label surface

lightAmbient.use: ambient radiance; same cool fill in both themes, not a foreground
lightAmbient.sameAs: graphOrigin.wikilink on dark; radiance remains unchanged on light

lightKey.use: key radiance; white light in both themes, not a foreground

lightRim.use: violet rim radiance in both themes, not a foreground

theme.use: browser theme-color; update alongside DOM and canvas on theme resolution

focus.use: visible focus ring for controls and selected outlines; pair with offset
focus.sameAs: accent.soft on dark; accent.base on light

$comment: Two curves, and no more. No `ease-in` anywhere — starting slow reads as lag
— and no overshoot, which argues with anything physically simulated on a
canvas behind it.

out.use: the default: decelerate into rest. Anything entering or settling

inOut.use: symmetric movement — something that slides both ways

$comment: DURATION SCALES WITH DISTANCE TRAVELLED, not with importance. A hover fill
travels 0px; a tooltip 4px; a panel 320px. That rule is what makes the
numbers predictable rather than a matter of taste.
Two pairs live here and they behave differently on purpose:
base/exit — a thing that ENTERS the page eases in at 180ms and leaves at
100ms. A slow exit is the most common way an interface comes to feel
sluggish, so exit is always faster than its enter.
in/out — HOVER and focus, which are the exception and invert that. Enter
is 0ms: a hover transition is feedback about your own pointer, whose
position you already know, and easing it in adds latency to the one
interaction that must feel free. Exit is 140ms because the pointer has
gone and nothing waits on it — the fade is what stops a fast mouse
crossing twenty rows from strobing.
Both relationships are asserted, so a later edit that 'tidies' the hover
pair into a symmetric one fails rather than shipping.

in.use: hover and focus ENTER — instant on purpose, never eased

out.use: hover and focus EXIT — the fade that stops flicker across rows

fast.use: a few px of travel: a chevron, a checkbox, a colour change

base.use: the default — tooltips, dropdowns, tens of px of travel

exit.use: the exit of a base transition; faster than the enter it reverses

slow.use: hundreds of px: a drawer or panel crossing the viewport

$comment: Elevation you can see. Reserved for popovers and above — a shadow on a
resting card competes with the surface ramp, which is the real elevation
signal in this system.
THE ALPHAS ARE TUNED ON THE DARK GROUND, because that is the only ground
with a production surface to derive them from. They are not wrong on light,
but they are heavier than a light scheme wants, and solving them properly
means measuring a real light surface rather than guessing. Guessing is
exactly what this package exists to stop, so they are shipped as one value
and the gap is recorded here rather than papered over.
`lip` is the odd one and the most useful: a 1px inset line along a panel's
TOP edge. That is what the eye actually reads as 'in front'. It works over
a moving canvas where a drop shadow does not, it costs nothing, and it is
derived from the text token's `-rgb` companion rather than a literal — so
it follows the scheme instead of being a second hardcoded colour.

soft.use: barely lifted: a dragged row, a sticky header hairline

base.use: popovers, menus, anything that floats over a surface

strong.use: modals and sheets — the top of the stack

lip.use: the specular top edge that reads as 'in front'; pair with any shadow

lipStrong.use: the same lip on a modal, where the edge has to carry more weight

$comment: The stacking order, named. Four overlay families sit over the page and an
ad-hoc `z-10` sprinkled at each call site is precisely how they end up
fighting — a tooltip under a modal, a toast behind a drawer.
Steps of 10 so a surface can slot something between two layers without
renumbering the scale, and unitless integers so they can be used in CSS and
in a style object without conversion.

canvas.use: the page and anything painted directly on it

modal.use: dialogs and sheets, above their own scrim

toast.use: transient notifications — above a modal, never blocked by one

tooltip.use: the top of the stack; nothing may cover a tooltip
